status_reasoning: The experimental design and data collection are well-supported. The optimized growth medium (C17), physiologically comparable time points (C18), high-quality microarray data validated by RNA-Seq (C101, C102), and high reproducibility (C106) collectively demonstrate robust experimental methodology for measuring mRNA profiles across 15 species (C1).

The correlation between transcriptional divergence and phylogenetic distance is well-supported by statistical analysis (C20, C26). The finding holds across different time points (C27, C28) and is not confounded by growth rate effects (C91, C92). The significant correlations even between distant species (C93) and low correlation despite similar lifestyle (C94) strengthen the conclusion.

The Arboretum algorithm and its application are well-justified. The method incorporates phylogenetic relationships (C30, C31, C32), the choice of k=5 modules is conservative and validated (C97, C98, C99), and the identification of five major modules across all species (C22) is supported by the computational framework (C19, C95, C96).

Module divergence proportional to phylogenetic distance is well-supported. The AMCI metric (C37) shows significant negative correlation with branch length (C38), and modules conserve membership inversely to phylogenetic distance (C36). This supports both the general finding (C2) and the specific observation about gene membership divergence (C23).

The characterization of the five modules is well-supported by data. Module 1 (growth/ribosome biogenesis, C33) and Module 5 (respiration/stress, C34) are the most conserved (C39, C41), while Modules 2-4 show intermediate patterns and lower stability (C35, C40). This is based on direct analysis of module assignments and stability metrics.

Coordinated reassignment of functionally related genes associated with lifestyle and ploidy changes is well-supported. Multiple gene sets (cell cycle C42, mating/meiosis C43, mitochondrial C44, oxidative phosphorylation C45, amino acid/purine metabolism C46) show phylogenetically coherent transitions (C47) that correlate with known lifestyle differences, supporting the general claim (C3).

Cis-regulatory changes accompanying module reassignment are well-supported. Nucleosome occupancy differences (C48), motif repositioning (C49), loss of Sfp1 sites (C50, C51), and convergent changes in both respiro-fermentative lineages (C66) with WGD-specific changes (C67) provide multiple lines of evidence for regulatory rewiring at the cis-regulatory level.

The contribution of paralogs to regulatory divergence within a short window after duplication is strongly supported. Statistical tests show paralogs are more likely to be reassigned than singletons (C54, C55), with ~53-60% reassigning at their point of origin (C59, C60). Enrichment analysis confirms this is specific to the duplication point (C61), supporting the 'window of opportunity' model (C62) and the general claims (C4, C24).

The prolonged contribution of WGD paralogs is well-supported. WGD paralogs show enrichment at both the WGD ancestor and later points (C63), with prominent divergence at A5 and A13 (C56) where more paralogs are retained (C57) and enriched in carbon metabolism (C58). The mechanistic explanation based on regulatory region preservation (C64, C65) is reasonable, supporting the general claims (C5, C25).

The classification of paralog fates is well-supported by data. The proportions of different fates (C73-C77) are based on systematic analysis of module assignments. The enrichment of neo-functionalized genes in unchanged modules (C78) and the inference about gaining regulation (C79) are reasonable. The contribution to carbon metabolism evolution (C80) is supported by data and consistent with cited work.

The generality of evolutionary patterns is supported by heat shock data. Similar patterns in phylogenetic distance correlation (C81), module conservation (C82), and paralog behavior (C83) across two independent conditions strongly support the inference that these are general principles (C84), validating the abstract claim (C6).

The rewiring of nucleotide biosynthesis pathways in post-WGD species is well-supported. Module reassignment of purine and amino acid metabolism genes (C52), involvement of WGD paralogs (C53), gradual changes visible in K. polysporus (C68), and analogy to cancer metabolism (C71) collectively support the inference that this rewiring contributes to the respiro-fermentative phenotype (C72).

The refined classification of paralog fates using two conditions is well-supported. The data show different patterns (C86-C89) that could not be distinguished with a single condition, validating the methodological inference (C85) that multiple conditions allow better classification of evolutionary outcomes.

While the analogy between respiro-fermentation and the Warburg effect is conceptually interesting and supported by citations (C69, C70), and the observation of similar pathway changes is data-driven (C71), the functional significance and mechanistic parallels remain speculative. The analogy is suggestive but would require additional experimental validation to be fully supported.

While S. japonicus and S. castellii show divergent lag phase profiles including anti-correlation in some cases, the manuscript notes that additional profiling at finer time increments did not change this finding. However, the possibility remains that the 30-minute fixed time point for lag phase may not capture the true physiologically comparable state in these divergent species, creating uncertainty about whether this represents true biological divergence or a sampling artifact.
